title: Migrants take jobs that would otherwise go to Australian-born workers
oneLiner: The oldest argument against migration, stated plainly.
body: Each job filled by a migrant is, on this view, a job not filled by someone already here. Supporters of a cap argue that lower migration would push employers to train and hire locally and lift wages for Australian workers.
contextBackground: The claim is widely held and almost never made by economists, who generally find that migrants add demand as well as supply and that the net effect on local employment is small. It is included because it circulates, and the community's rating of it is informative.
contextDisagreement: The claim treats the number of jobs as fixed. Critics argue that is the error: migrants also spend, start businesses and fill roles that enable other jobs. Whether low-wage local workers are an exception is the one point of genuine dispute.

otherClaim.title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year

claimItself.title: Net overseas migration should be held below 200,000 a year
claimItself.oneLiner: Whether the federal government should cap net arrivals below the levels of the past decade and well below the post-pandemic peak.
claimItself.body: Net overseas migration is arrivals minus departures of people who stay, or leave, for at least twelve months. It averaged just over 200,000 a year in the decade before the pandemic and exceeded 500,000 in 2022–23. The proposal is a cap of 200,000, which would require the government to manage the student, temporary-work and permanent programs together to hit it.
